title: Mendelian Inheritance
hook: A 19th-century monk breeding pea plants worked out the hidden rules of heredity — why a trait can skip a generation and reappear in your grandchild.
key_points: We inherit two copies of each gene, one from each parent; versions are called alleles.
A dominant allele shows its trait even if only one copy is present.
A recessive allele's trait appears only when both copies are recessive.
A Punnett square predicts the odds of each combination in offspring.
content_html: Long before anyone knew about DNA, a monk named Gregor Mendel cracked the basic math of heredity by carefully breeding thousands of pea plants. His insight: traits are passed down in discrete units (what we now call genes), in predictable ratios. It explains familiar mysteries, like why a trait can vanish in parents and reappear in their children.
extra_html: The core idea is that you carry two copies of each gene, and the versions are called alleles. A dominant allele shows its effect even if you have just one copy, while a recessive allele's trait appears only when you inherit two recessive copies. That's why a recessive trait can hide for a generation and then resurface. To predict the odds, geneticists use a Punnett square — a grid that crosses the parents' alleles to show the probability of each outcome in their offspring. Encyclopaedia Britannica's overview of Mendelism traces how these rules, drawn from pea plants, became the foundation of modern genetics.

related.title: How Genes Become Traits
related.hook: You inherit two copies of every gene — one from each parent — and the way those copies interact helps decide everything from eye color to blood type.

related.title: Chromosomes and Meiosis
related.hook: Your DNA is packed into 46 bundles called chromosomes — and a special kind of cell division halves that number so sperm and egg can combine without doubling up.

flashcards.back_html: One of the different versions of a gene. You inherit two alleles for each gene — one from each parent — and they may match or differ.

flashcards.prompt: A recessive trait shows up only when...

choices.text: Both copies of the gene are the recessive allele
At least one copy is the recessive allele
The dominant allele is also present

flashcards.explanation_html: A recessive trait appears only when both alleles are recessive. A single dominant allele is enough to mask it.

flashcards.prompt: What is a Punnett square used for?

choices.text: Predicting the probability of offspring's traits
Measuring the length of a chromosome

flashcards.explanation_html: A Punnett square is a simple grid that combines the parents' alleles to show the chances of each possible trait in their offspring.
